newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Jews weigh inquiry into Swiss role in WW2.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Jews weigh inquiry into Swiss role in WW2.

text.p: Leading Jewish groups said on Monday they were considering establishing a special committee, in partnership with the Israeli government, to investigate Swiss involvement in World War Two.

The Jewish Agency and the World Jewish Congress said the new investigation would follow an international inquiry into whether Swiss banks are hiding funds Jewish victims of the Nazi holocaust stashed away to keep from Hitler.

"Jewish Agency Chairman Avraham Burg and World Jewish Congress Secretary General Israel Singer said today they will consider establishing a special committee in partnership with the Israeli government to hold an independent investigation into Swiss involvement in World War Two," a Jewish Agency statement said.
"Without access to the proceedings or operating criteria of the newly-proposed Swiss committee, we are concerned that there could be an attempt to rewrite history," the statement said.
"Such a step would turn the current proceedings of the international commission headed by Paul Volcker into a rubber stamp based on an incorrect historical understanding."
A panel examining whether Swiss banks are sitting on riches of Holocaust victims will meet in Zurich this month to discuss the destruction of documents by one of the banks, Burg said.
"The international commission...will meet at the end of this month in Zurich for a special discussion regarding the destruction of documents by the Union Bank of Switzerland," he said.

Burg serves on the independent Swiss-Jewish panel led by former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker looking into the charges by the World Jewish Congress and other groups that Swiss were holding holocaust victims's money.
Commission members had earlier said they would meet in Zurich on January 31 but without detailing the agenda.

The panel aims to put to rest Jewish groups' suspicions about the banks' credibility, reinforced when it emerged last week that Union Bank of Switzerland had had shredded some old documents from a subsidiary it acquired in 1945.

Thomas Borer, head of the government task force coordinating Switzerland's response to critics, said he was still awaiting a Zurich district attorney's report on the case, which came to light when a guard smuggled out some papers to Jewish leaders.
In a statement issued in Jerusalem, Burg said Volcker had notified the six commission members he intended to invite Swiss banking and government representatives to the meeting.
"This session is another victory for morality and justice," Burg said. "We will go bank by bank until we discover exactly who destroyed how much and when."
He demanded an auditor and investigators appointed by the panel enter each of the Swiss banks in surprise "spot checks".
"The UBS suspicions raise the most severe moral implications for all of Swiss banking," Burg said. "If we substantiate the suspicions, I will have many questions to ask the Swiss banking heads."
Prosecutors are now investigating whether UBS broke a ban on destroying relevant records or if the guard violated Swiss banking secrecy. UBS said the destruction of the records was an accident.
Six million Jews were systematically killed in the holocaust by the Nazis under Hitler during World War Two.
